title: Home at last
hookLine: airport goodbyes, a door closing, and the first word at the gate of the Garden
tomorrow: what if four little words were the whole map?

lines: A DOOR CLOSES, A DOOR OPENS.
cards: Airport goodbyes have their own script. One more hug. Text me when you land.
Did you pack your charger? Then a door closes behind you, and somewhere else, another door opens.
The Qur'an describes the gates of the Garden, and the first word said there is one Muslims already say at every door: peace.
The angels come in from every gate, it says, in Pickthall's words: "Peace be unto you because ye persevered."

teach.b: Peace runs all through the Qur'an's picture of the Garden.

In one place, its people hear no idle talk there and no blame, only the saying: peace, and again peace. In another, their greeting there is: peace. Allah, the Qur'an says, calls to the abode of peace, dar al-salam.
That's today's line: peace, peace. And notice that it's a homecoming word.
A verse tells Muslims to greet one another when they enter houses, with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good, and so as-salamu alaykum is said walking through front doors every evening.
Every one of those is a small rehearsal of the last door. The Qur'an doesn't picture the Garden as a hotel you check into alone.
The same passage about the gates says the righteous of their parents, spouses and children enter with them.
Family, gathered in, and a greeting at the gate. Look closely at the gate: the angels don't just say welcome.
They say peace, because you kept going.

how: Muslims greet with as-salamu alaykum when entering a home, following Qur'an 24:61, and speak of the Garden as dar al-salam, the abode of peace, where the Qur'an says the greeting is peace.

o: the Garden as a home, greeted at the gate with peace
finally moving back into your family's house
the moment the soul rests in the grave after burial

games.q: peace in the Qur'an — tap the pairs.
p: peace be unto you, ye persevered
greet with a greeting from Allah

s: the Qur'an pictures the Garden as a place you enter alone
the passage about the gates says the righteous of their parents, spouses and children enter with them.
in the Qur'an, the angels at the gate say: peace be unto you because ye persevered
'peace' is a word saved for the Garden, not for every day
a verse tells Muslims to greet when they enter houses; every front door is a small rehearsal.

games.q: you get back to your empty apartment after a long day. nobody's there. what does a verse in the Qur'an say about entering houses?
o: greet with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good.
say nothing unless someone is there to answer.
wait until someone greets you, then return it.
games.why: 24:61 tells Muslims to greet when they enter houses, with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good. some say salaam even to an empty room.

practice: If you can, get up and walk slowly to the nearest door. Rest your hand on it for a breath, and as you step through, say salaam, or simply the word peace, to whoever is there, or to the empty room. Walk back the same slow way.

wordCard.voice: Home at last: the Garden as the Qur'an pictures it, a home with family gathered in, where the greeting at the gate is peace.

orig.note: Arabic: peace; the greeting of the Garden, and of every front door.

carryVoice: Two words for every doorway: peace, peace, said here and said at the last gate. The journey home is complete.

sources.q: Peace be unto you because ye persevered.

sources.ref: Qur'an 13:23: the righteous of their fathers, spouses and offspring enter with them; the angels enter from every gate
Qur'an 56:25–26: no idle talk nor blame, only the saying peace, peace; 10:10: their greeting there is peace; 10:25: Allah calls to the abode of peace
Qur'an 24:61: when you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good
